title: Advanced HTML & CSS
intro: This term you will learn the pro tools web designers use: Grid, Flexbox, animations and SASS. Step by step, you will build a real, lively website for a local food business.
termProject: A feature-rich, animated, phone-friendly website for 'Mama Titi's Jollof Spot', a buka in Ilaro, using real menu and brand info from your research.

weeks.title: Grid: Arrange the Food Tray
weeks.goal: I can use CSS Grid to place menu cards in neat rows and columns.
weeks.learn: CSS Grid cuts your page into rows and columns, like a tray of puff-puff. You tell the box 'display: grid' and say how many columns you want. 'repeat(2, 1fr)' means two equal columns. 'gap' puts space between cards so they don't touch. Every card now sits in its own spot by itself.

research.q: Ask a food seller near you: what are your 4 best-selling foods?
research.tip: Write the 4 food names down — they become the cards on your Mama Titi menu this term.

build.task: Make a 2-column grid of four food cards for Mama Titi's Jollof Spot.
steps: Make a div with class 'menu' and put 4 card divs inside.
Give .menu 'display: grid'.
Add 'grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr)'.
Add a gap and press Run.
build.code:
Mama Titi's Jollof Spot

Jollof Rice
₦1,500
Fried Plantain
₦500
Moi Moi
₦400
Chicken
₦1,200

check.q: Which line turns a box into a grid?

weeks.say: I used CSS Grid to arrange food cards in two neat columns like a tray.

trainer.open: Look at an egg crate: every egg has its own spot. Today we build an egg crate for our menu with CSS Grid.
plan: Show an egg crate or picture; ask why eggs don't roll around.
Explain display: grid, columns and gap on the board.
Kids type the menu grid and change 2 columns to 3.
Share research: which foods sell most near you?
props: An egg crate or picture of one
Food price list from a local buka
lookfor: Changes the number of columns without help
Explains what 1fr means in own words
Adjusts gap to make space bigger or smaller
fix: Puts display: grid on the cards, not the parent
Say: the tray is the grid, not the eggs. Move it to .menu.
Writes 'repeat(2 1fr)' without a comma
Point to the comma and say: repeat needs a comma between the count and size.

weeks.title: Flexbox: Line Up Like a Danfo
weeks.goal: I can use Flexbox to line up a menu bar and spread items across the page.
weeks.learn: Flexbox puts items in one line, like passengers sitting in a danfo row. 'display: flex' lines up the children side by side. 'justify-content: space-between' pushes them apart to the edges. 'align-items: center' keeps them level in the middle. Grid is for the full tray; Flexbox is for one row.

research.q: Ask a shop owner: what 3 things must a customer see first on a sign or website?
research.tip: Write the 3 things down — they will go in your navigation bar.

build.task: Build a navigation bar for Mama Titi's site with Flexbox.
steps: Make a nav with a logo and 3 links.
Give nav 'display: flex'.
Add 'justify-content: space-between' and 'align-items: center'.
Run it and try 'space-around' too.
build.code:
Mama Titi 🍛
MenuPricesCall

opts: Items in one row or column

check.q: Which property spreads items to the edges?

weeks.say: I used Flexbox to line up my menu bar like passengers in one danfo row.

trainer.open: In a danfo, passengers sit in one row and the conductor shifts them. Today Flexbox is our conductor!
plan: Line 4 kids in a row; ask them to spread out, then bunch in the centre.
Link the movement to justify-content and align-items.
Kids build the nav bar and test 3 justify-content values.
Share research: what must customers see first?
props: 4 chairs for a 'danfo row'
Picture of a shop signboard
lookfor: Says when to use Grid and when to use Flexbox
fix: Mixes up justify-content and align-items
Say: justify goes along the row (left-right), align goes up-down.
Puts display: flex on the links
Remind them: the parent (nav) gets flex, the children line up inside.

weeks.title: Responsive: Fits Every Phone
weeks.goal: I can use a media query so my page changes for small phones and big screens.
weeks.learn: A responsive page changes shape for the screen, like a tailor who adjusts one dress for different sizes. A media query is a rule: IF the screen is wider than 600px, THEN use 4 columns. On small phones we stay with 1 column. This is called 'mobile first'. The meta viewport tag tells the phone to show the real size.

research.q: Ask 3 people: do you mostly browse on a phone or a computer?
research.tip: Count the answers — it shows why we design for phones first.

build.task: Make the Mama Titi menu show 1 column on phones and 4 on wide screens.
steps: Add the meta viewport tag.
Set .menu to 1 column by default.
Add '@media (min-width: 600px)' with 4 columns.
Turn your phone sideways or zoom out to test.
build.code:
Jollof ₦1,500
Plantain ₦500
Moi Moi ₦400
Chicken ₦1,200

opts: A rule: IF the screen is big, THEN change

check.q: What does the meta viewport tag do?
opts: Tells the phone to show the real size

weeks.say: I made my page responsive, like a tailor adjusting one dress for every size.

trainer.open: A tailor sews one style but adjusts it for every body. Today our page learns to adjust for every screen.
plan: Show a page on a phone and on a big screen; ask what changed.
Explain media queries as IF rules (red logic colour).
Kids add the media query and test by rotating the phone.
Tally research: phone vs computer users.
props: A tape measure
Two devices of different sizes if possible
lookfor: Explains a media query as an IF rule
Changes the breakpoint number and predicts the result
fix: Forgets the closing } of the @media block
Count the brackets together: every { needs a }.
Uses max-width and gets confused
Say: min-width means 'from this size and bigger'. Start with that.

weeks.title: Make It Move: Transitions & Keyframes
weeks.goal: I can add a smooth hover transition and a repeating keyframe animation.
weeks.learn: A transition makes a change happen slowly, like a gate swinging open instead of slamming. 'transition: 0.3s' smooths changes when you hover or tap. A keyframe animation is a little story: start here, end there. 'infinite' makes it repeat again and again, like a fan blade turning.

research.q: Ask a trader: what makes you notice a shop sign from far away?
research.tip: Write their answer — movement and colour help customers notice an 'Order Now' button.

build.task: Make an 'Order Now' button that grows on tap and a hot-food icon that bounces.
steps: Add a button and give it 'transition: transform 0.3s'.
Add ':hover' and ':active' to scale it up.
Write '@keyframes bounce' with from and to.
Attach the animation to the 🍲 icon with 'infinite'.
build.code:
🍲

Hot Jollof Ready!

check.q: Which word makes an animation repeat forever?
Where do you write the steps of an animation?

weeks.say: I made my Order button grow smoothly and my food icon bounce forever.

trainer.open: A gate that slams scares you; a gate that swings is smooth. Today we make our buttons swing, not slam.
plan: Open and close a door fast, then slowly; ask which looks nicer.
Explain transition (purple: tap event) and keyframes with infinite (green: repeat).
Kids build the button and bouncing icon; change speed from 0.8s to 0.3s.
Share research: what makes a sign catch your eye?
props: A door or a toy gate
A table fan to show repeating motion
lookfor: Changes the animation speed and explains the effect
fix: Writes the animation name differently in @keyframes and animation
Say: the names must match exactly, like a password.
Puts transition only inside :hover

weeks.title: Animate.css: Ready-Made Moves
weeks.goal: I can link the Animate.css library and use its ready-made animation classes.
weeks.learn: A CSS library is code someone else already wrote, like buying ready-made pepper soup spice instead of grinding it yourself. Animate.css gives you moves like bounce, fadeIn and pulse. You link it with one <link> tag from a CDN. Then you add two classes: 'animate__animated' and the move you want, like 'animate__bounceIn'.

research.q: Ask an adult: what ready-made thing do you buy to save time when cooking?
research.tip: Write it down — it's the same idea as using a library instead of writing everything yourself.

build.task: Link Animate.css and make Mama Titi's welcome sign bounce in.
steps: Paste the Animate.css <link> tag in the head.
Give your h1 the classes 'animate__animated animate__bounceIn'.
Give a paragraph 'animate__fadeInUp' with a delay class.
Press Run again to replay.
build.code:
Welcome to Mama Titi's!

Hot jollof, sweet plantain, every day in Ilaro.

🔥 Open now

check.q: Which TWO classes make Animate.css work?
opts: animate__animated plus a move like animate__bounceIn

check.q: How do we add Animate.css to our page?

weeks.say: I used Animate.css, a ready-made library, to make my sign bounce in with one class.

trainer.open: Who here has used ready-made Maggi or spice? Today we use ready-made animations!

Show the CDN link and the two-class pattern.
Kids try 3 different moves: bounceIn, fadeInUp, pulse.
Share research: ready-made things adults buy to save time.
props: A seasoning cube

lookfor: Swaps one animation name for another correctly
fix: Forgets the 'animate__animated' class

weeks.title: Tap to Animate: Interactive Effects
weeks.goal: I can combine Animate.css with hover and tap effects to make interactive menu cards.
weeks.learn: Interactive means the page answers you when you touch it, like a POS beeping when you press a key. We can start an Animate.css move only when a user hovers or taps a card. We use ':hover' and ':active' in our own CSS to switch on the library's animation. This makes the menu feel alive.

research.q: Ask a POS agent: how do customers know their button press worked?
research.tip: Write their answer — a beep or flash is 'feedback', and our cards need it too.

build.task: Make menu cards that 'tada' when you hover or tap them.
steps: Link Animate.css.
Make cards with class 'card'.
In your CSS, on '.card:hover' and '.card:active', set 'animation-name: tada'.
Add 'animation-duration: 1s' and test by tapping.

weeks.title: SASS Variables & Nesting
weeks.goal: I can explain SASS variables and nesting and read the CSS they turn into.
weeks.learn: SASS is a helper language that makes CSS shorter, like writing 'Mama' instead of her full name every time. A variable like '$brand: #c0392b;' stores a colour once so you can reuse it. Nesting lets you write 'nav { a { } }' to show that links live inside the nav. Browsers can't read SASS, so a tool compiles it into normal CSS, which is what runs below.

research.q: Ask a business owner: what are your brand colours (on your sign, bags or uniform)?
research.tip: Write the colours — you'll store them as SASS variables for Mama Titi's site.

build.task: Read the SCSS in the comment, then see its compiled CSS run as a branded nav.
steps: Read the SCSS: find the $brand variable and the nesting.
Look at the compiled CSS below it and match each line.
Change the colour in the compiled CSS (where $brand was used).
Run and say which SASS line made which CSS line.
build.code: MenuPricesCall Mama Titi

opts: Stores a colour in a variable

weeks.say: I learnt that SASS variables store colours once and nesting shows what lives inside what.

trainer.open: If Mama Titi changes her brand colour, do we want to change it in 50 places or in 1? SASS lets us change 1.
plan: Ask: if your nickname changed, would you rewrite every exercise book?
Explain variables and nesting; show SCSS beside compiled CSS.
Kids match SCSS lines to CSS lines, then change the brand colour.
Share research: real brand colours from local businesses.
props: A labelled jar (variable = label, contents = value)
Printed SCSS vs CSS sheet
lookfor: Points to where a variable's value appears in the CSS
fix: Thinks the browser reads the $ variables
Show that the comment is ignored; only the compiled lines run.
Forgets the space in 'nav a'
Say: the space means 'a inside nav'. Without it, the rule breaks.

weeks.title: SASS Mixins: One Recipe, Many Pots
weeks.goal: I can explain a SASS mixin and see how it repeats the same styles in many places.
weeks.learn: A mixin is a saved style recipe, like Mama's jollof recipe she reuses for every party. You write '@mixin card-style { }' once. Then '@include card-style;' pastes it into any rule. You can even pass a value, like a colour, so each pot comes out a bit different. The compiler copies the recipe into the CSS for you.

research.q: Ask an adult cook: which recipe do you repeat the same way for every party?
research.tip: Write the recipe name — a mixin is the coding version of that repeated recipe.

build.task: Read a mixin with a colour value and see it compiled into two different buttons.
steps: Find '@mixin pill($bg)' in the SCSS comment.
Find the two '@include' lines.
Look at the compiled .order and .call rules — same recipe, different colour.
Add a third button style in the compiled CSS following the same recipe.
build.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
<style>
/* SCSS:
   @mixin pill($bg) { background: $bg; color: white;
     padding: 12px 20px; border-radius: 30px; border: none; }
   .order { @include pill(#27ae60); }
   .call  { @include pill(#2980b9); }
   Compiled CSS: */
.order { background: #27ae60; color: white; padding: 12px 20px; border-radius: 30px; border: none; }
.call  { background: #2980b9; color: white; padding: 12px 20px; border-radius: 30px; border: none; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
  <button class="order">Order Jollof</button>
  <button class="call">Call Mama Titi</button>
</body>
</html>

weeks.say: A mixin is a style recipe I write once and include anywhere, changing only the colour.

trainer.open: Mama cooks jollof the same way for every owambe, just adding more pepper sometimes. That is a mixin!
plan: Ask about a family recipe that is repeated for every party.
Kids trace the recipe into compiled CSS and add a third button.
Compare mixins (repeat = green) and variables (data = blue).
props: A written recipe card
Two cups of different colours
lookfor: Writes a correct third button rule
fix: Thinks @mixin alone adds styles
Say: writing the recipe doesn't cook; @include is when you cook it.
Mixes up variables and mixins
Variable = one value; mixin = a group of style lines.

weeks.title: Complex Layouts with Grid Areas
weeks.goal: I can build a full page layout with header, menu, sidebar and footer using grid areas.
weeks.learn: Big websites have many parts, like a market with sections for pepper, fabric and phones. 'grid-template-areas' lets you draw your page with words. You name each part, like 'head', 'menu', 'side' and 'foot'. Then you tell each box which area it belongs to. On phones we stack them; on big screens they sit side by side.

research.q: Visit or picture your local market: what sections does it have and where is each one?
research.tip: Draw a small map — your page layout is a map with named sections too.

build.task: Lay out Mama Titi's full page with named grid areas.
steps: Give .page 'display: grid'.
Draw the areas with words in 'grid-template-areas'.
Give each part a 'grid-area' name.
Run and swap the 'menu' and 'side' words to see them move.
build.code:

Menu: Jollof, Plantain, Moi Moi
Open 8am–8pm
Ilaro, Ogun State

trainer.open: Every market has a map in the traders' heads: pepper here, fabric there. Today we draw a map for our website.

weeks.title: Showcase: Mama Titi's Full Website
weeks.goal: I can combine Grid, Flexbox, media queries, animations and SASS ideas into one feature-rich page.
weeks.learn: Today we put every skill on one plate, like a full owambe party pack: rice, plantain, chicken and drink. Grid arranges the menu. Flexbox lines up the nav. A media query fixes it for phones. Animations make it lively. Our colours come from SASS-style variables, written here as CSS custom properties so it runs in the browser.

research.q: Show your page to a food seller or family member: what one thing would make them order?
research.tip: Write their answer — real feedback is how real websites improve.

build.task: Finish a feature-rich website for Mama Titi's Jollof Spot.
steps: Set brand colours as variables in :root.
Add the Flexbox nav and the Grid menu.
Add a media query for wide screens.
Add the Animate.css welcome and a hover effect, then show someone.
